kinds.d: Beryllium aluminium silicate mineral specimen: hexagonal crystals in all colours; named varieties are listed as archetypes. Cut stones are under Gemstones & pearls.

x.d: Green beryl coloured mainly by chromium; classic Colombian crystals from Muzo, Coscuez and Chivor.
x.dt: crystal in calcite matrix · miniature to cabinet

x.d: Blue to cyan beryl coloured by iron; crystals from Minas Gerais, Pakistan, Mount Antero (Colorado) and elsewhere.
Pink to rose beryl coloured by manganese, also called cesian or pink beryl.
Yellow to gold beryl coloured by Fe³⁺; the largest cut golden beryl weighs 2,054 carats.
Colourless beryl named after Goshen, Massachusetts; irradiation gives other colours.
Rare manganese-coloured red beryl (bixbite), first described in 1904 at Maynard's Claim, Juab County, Utah.
Deep-blue beryl coloured by radiation-induced colour centres.
Record crystals: Bumpus Quarry, Albany, Maine (about 18 tonnes) and Malakialina, Madagascar (18 m, about 380,000 kg).

v.d: largest natural crystal of any mineral

kinds.d: Aluminium fluorosilicate mineral specimen: orthorhombic prisms in colourless, blue, yellow, pink and imperial orange.

x.d: Yellow, pink or pink-orange topaz, golden brown from Brazil; the most valued colours.
Natural blue is rare; pale stones are heat-treated and irradiated to a darker blue.
Topaz from Topaz Mountain, Juab County, Utah, in vapour cavities in rhyolite.
Topaz from Ghundao Hill (Katlang) and the Skardu and Gilgit districts, Pakistan.
Topaz from Mursinka and the Ilmen Mountains, Russia, first found about the 1700s.
Large blue topaz from the St Ann's mine, Zimbabwe, found in the late 1980s.
Colourless topaz coated by vapour deposition to give a rainbow surface.

kinds.d: Zirconium silicate mineral specimen: brown to red tetragonal crystals; also the oldest dated minerals on Earth.

x.d: Yellow, orange and red zircon, named after the flower hyacinthus.
Light-coloured zircon.
Zircons from Jack Hills, Western Australia, dated up to 4.404 billion years, the oldest dated minerals on Earth.
Radiation-damaged zircon with lowered density and greasy lustre.
Heat-treated brown zircon from Ratanakiri, Cambodia, heated to about 800–1,000 °C; sometimes sold as cambolite.
Large zircon crystals from Mud Tank, Valley Bore, Northern Territory.
Zircon crystals from Larvik and Hakedal, Norway, and the Ilmen Mountains, Russia.

kinds.d: Magnesium-rich olivine mineral specimen; the gem variety is peridot, treated under Peridot.

x.d: Gem-quality forsterite crystals from Zabargad, Pakistan (Sapat, Naran), Myanmar and Arizona.
Type-locality forsterite from Monte Somma, Vesuvius; named in 1824 for Adolarius Forster.
Large forsterite crystals from the Kovdor massif, Kola Peninsula.
Olivine in volcanic bombs; Eifel and Arizona (Buell Park).

kinds.d: Barium titanium silicate mineral specimen: blue triangular crystals from San Benito County, California; fluoresces blue under short-wave UV.

x.d: Benitoite from the Benitoite Gem mine, San Benito County; discovered 1907 by James Couch, identified 1909 by George Louderback.
x.dt: blue crystals on natrolite · thumbnail to miniature · UV-fluorescent

x.d: Benitoite from the Gem mine, Mina Numero Uno, the Victor and Junilla claims and Santa Rita Peak.
Benitoite from the Diamond Jo quarry, Magnet Cove, Arkansas.
Benitoite from Ohmi, Niigata, Japan.

kinds.d: Aluminium silicate mineral specimen: blue blades with hardness that differs by direction.

x.d: Bladed blue kyanite crystals; hardness 5.5 along the length and 7 across.
Euhedral kyanite crystals from Pizzo Forno and Alpe Sponda, Ticino, Switzerland.
Large kyanite crystals from Minas Gerais pegmatites.
Manganese-coloured orange kyanite from Loliondo, Tanzania.
Kyanite from Mt Greiner, Zillertal, Austria.

kinds.d: Aluminium silicate mineral specimen: pleochroic prisms and cross-patterned chiastolite.

x.d: Andalusite with dark carbon or clay inclusions forming a cross in cross-section; carried as a souvenir by Santiago pilgrims from at least the 16th century.
Green manganese-bearing andalusite.
Clear pleochroic andalusite from Brazil and Sri Lanka showing red, green and yellow flashes.
Andalusite from the Lisens Alp, Selraintal, Tirol.

kinds.d: Iron aluminium silicate mineral specimen: brown crystals with cruciform 'fairy cross' twins.

x.d: Staurolite penetration twins at 60° or 90°; Fairy Stone State Park, Patrick County, Virginia is named after it.
Staurolite from Fannin County, Georgia, where it is the state mineral.
Staurolite from Pizzo Forno and Alpe Piona, Ticino, and Mt Greiner, Zillertal.
Large staurolite twins from the old provinces of Finistère and Morbihan, Brittany.

kinds.d: Calcium borosilicate mineral specimen: colourless to pale yellow wedge-shaped crystals.

x.d: Type-locality danburite from Danbury, Connecticut, discovered in 1839 by Charles Upham Shepard.
Large danburite crystals from Charcas, San Luis Potosí, Mexico.
Very large danburite crystals from Anjanabonoina and Mt Bity, Madagascar.
Danburite from Dal'negorsk, Primorsky Krai, Russia.
Danburite from the Mogok district, Myanmar.

kinds.d: Magnesium aluminium silicate mineral specimen; the gem variety is iolite.

x.d: Transparent violet-blue cordierite with strong pleochroism, called water sapphire and Vikings' compass.
Cordierite first described in 1813 from Níjar, Almería, Spain, named after Louis Cordier.
Cordierite crystals from the gem gravels of Sri Lanka.
Cordierite from Bodenmais, Bavaria.

kinds.d: Beryllium aluminium silicate hydroxide mineral specimen: pale blue-green crystals with perfect cleavage.

x.d: Euclase from Minas Gerais, the type locality, found with topaz.
Large euclase crystals from the Gachalá mine near Chivor, Colombia.
Euclase from the Lost Hope mine, Mwami, Zimbabwe.
Euclase first reported in 1792 from gold-bearing gravels, Orenburg district, southern Urals.

kinds.d: Beryllium silicate mineral specimen: colourless glassy crystals that resemble quartz.

x.d: Phenakite from the Takovaya stream near Yekaterinburg and the Ilmen Mountains.
Phenakite from Mount Antero, Colorado, with aquamarine.
Large prismatic phenakite from a feldspar quarry near Kragerø, Norway.
Exceptional phenakite crystals from the São Miguel de Piracicaba pegmatite, Minas Gerais.
Phenakite from Anjanabonoina, Madagascar.

kinds.d: Calcium aluminium borosilicate group specimen: axe-shaped brown, violet or blue crystals (axinite-(Fe), -(Mg), -(Mn), tinzenite).

x.d: Iron end member (ferroaxinite): clove-brown, plum-blue or pearl-grey crystals.
Magnesium end member: pale blue to violet, light brown or pink.
Manganese end member: honey-yellow, clove-brown and brown to blue.
Iron-manganese intermediate in yellow to brownish yellow-green.
Axinite from the West Bor Pit, Dalnegorsk, Russia.
Axinite from the Wessels mine, Kalahari manganese fields, South Africa.

kinds.d: Magnesium aluminium borosilicate mineral specimen: rare bluish-green crystals, mainly from Madagascar.

x.d: Large grandidierite crystals from Andrahomana near Fort Dauphin, discovered in 1902 and named for Alfred Grandidier.
x.dt: cyan to turquoise crystals · gem rough

x.d: Cyan-to-turquoise transparent faceted stones, extremely rare in large sizes.
Grandidierite from the Kachebere Hills, Mchinji, Malawi.

notes: All 14 planned kinds kept. HOM has no axinite file (axinite-Fe 404) so Axinite relies on Wikipedia; Wikipedia pages used for varieties. Older gem varieties (emerald, aquamarine, etc.) appear as crystal archetypes with cut stones deferred to Gemstones & pearls. Not found on fetched pages and so omitted: Swiss/London blue topaz, starlite, Mexican items. No brands or traditions.
